Hello. I have, with very heavy AI assistance, produced a Lean 4 formalisation of the four colour theorem, following Gonthier and Werner's Coq proof.

I don't know if that's interesting to people or not, I'm not sure after recent events what the attitude is towards AI generated formal proofs etc. But hopefully it's useful or interesting to someone.

FourColor.fourColorTheorem depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound (no native_decide).

It broadly follows Gonthier's structure, but uses Mathlib for the mathematical foundation rather than transliterating MathComp, and deviates more significantly for computational reasons in how reducibility is proven and how the certificates are processed (heavy use of megabit-width Nat arithmetic as an acceleration, where the original uses Coq's bytecode VM instead — see the readme).

From a contribution standpoint:

  • The statement of the theorem is only 195 lines on top of Mathlib, making it easy to hand verify.
  • Demonstrates megabit-width Nat arithmetic as a way to make a computationally intensive proof feasible inside the kernel, without native_decide.

Here's the repo: https://github.com/corun1024/4ct

  • Chris Emery
I would advise you to set up your project with comparator and formalization.yaml.

Ah, interesting that there's been a previous AI assisted attempt, I wasn't aware of that. Possibly the difference between now and that attempt in April is simply a few AI model iterations. I originally was using Opus 5, but it seemed like it was struggling so bumped up to Fable 5.1.

My original interest was in seeing if an agent could come up with a much simpler proof of 4ct, but I wanted to start from a good starting point and have it try to simplify it, rather than starting from scratch and building up, then I discovered there was no proof in lean and then went down that rabbit hole :man_shrugging: .

Porting directly not so difficult (for ai). The issue is that the reducibility part of the proof has a lot of computation that lean is very slow at where rocq isn't so bad. So fable needed to rewrite that bit with some tricks. It takes advantage of that large Nat numbers in lean are backed by GMP which is very fast, and the proof packs a whole bunch of stuff into megabit-width nat numbers that it does operations on, to achieve decent performance.
@Chris Emery : Maybe this variant is also tractable with your approach. It will be presented at FOCS'26 in November: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24880

Worth a note since comparator support was requested that even exporting with lean4export looks like it would take about a day on my machine. Partly because single threaded and partly because it is rewriting all the megabit sized nat literals in decimal (they're hex in the source).

You could probably store them in a different way (like base 64 strings) that doesn’t get written to decimal in the export. Maybe you would need some converter that definitionally reduces to a list of nats.
(But maybe I’m not understanding the bottleneck.)
Also, you project says it requires python and gcc. What are those for?

@Jason Rute, For a kernel arena benchmark, it's extremely computation heavy, it takes about 1 core-hour to generate the generated parts of the proof (which is done with c and python, and results in lean files containing mostly just a bunch of bignums). The generated source is then 1.1 gigabytes. It then takes about 8 core-hours to check with lean.
For a benchmark, maybe then some subpart of the project, or a toy example, but @Joachim Breitner would know better. I haven’t thought this through.

(The build can be parallelised across modules but needs care because some modules peak at 8+ gig of memory usage. So naive parallelisation ends up running out of memory (on my system anyway). So, a build system is provided that builds knowns the peak memory usage of each module, you then provide it a max parallelism and max memory usage and it manages building the modules without exceeding your system's memory)
Extracted a few bits that could be used as kernel benchmarks potentially: https://github.com/corun1024/4ct_kernel_arena_benchmark
That looks like a nice benchmark/test, PR at the kernel arena is welcome
@Jason Rute @Chris Emery Preliminary results:
Can you include con-ron in the comparison? It has its own naive bignum implementation

Using the four colour theorem as a benchmark has historic precedent, it was also used as the benchmark in the paper on vm_compute in Rocq.

Using the VM was 33-35 times faster on a Pentium III 1Ghz with 256 Mb RAM than using the normalization algorithm of Rocq at the time :)

I learned about this when trying to find out whether as the README says the "bytecode virtual machine [was] added to Coq for this proof". Georges told me by email that actually the proof of the four color theorem was done without the VM. In fact, it was fully checked on Rocq Version 7.3.1 according to Georges' paper. This version of Rocq did not have a VM, see e.g. the doc or the code. It seems like the VM was added for V8.1 but not yet present in V8.0

Now in retrospect, it is actually a bit surprising to me that Lean's kernel cannot just do the same computation that ran in Rocq without a VM 25 years ago. Do we know what actually is the barrier in the Lean kernel? It seems to not be the lack of a VM!

Did Rocq's kernel already rely on its current abstract machine to do reduction 25 years ago, or did it use to have as naive an algorithm as Lean currently implements ?

I have no where near the background to understand if this sounds accurate, but I asked my Claude that had the context of doing this work. It says:

The Coq proof ran before vm_compute existed (that came in 8.0, 2004, and only sped it up). What made it feasible was that Coq's kernel reduction is an evaluator: a lazy abstract machine whose intermediate values are ordinary heap objects the GC reclaims. Lean 4's kernel doesn't evaluate; it decides defeq by whnf over Expr with a cache of every reduction performed. On this workload that means ~10 µs per step (vs well under 1 µs for Coq's lazy machine, tens of ns for its VM), and nothing allocated during a computation is freed until the declaration ends. A Kempe closure visiting ~10⁹ intermediate values therefore costs both hours and tens of GB per configuration. Our first scheme, close to the Coq design, did prove 87 configurations, but projected to ~90 core-hours with 60 GB peaks for all 633. native_decide would fix the speed but trusts the compiler (extra axiom), which we ruled out.

Note that I did actually let it explore using native_decide for a while anyway and it didn’t seem to provide that much performance improvement so I switched it in the bignum direction.

Have you tried checking the proof with sokonanoda (NbE) or nanoclo (delayed substitutions, I think)? I'm very curious if these perform significantly better here?
(see https://arena.lean-lang.org/)

Also works with lean4lean (no GMP) within lean (no GMP), about 30% slower, but I believe this could be optimized further.
However, it is not clear that this would really shrink the TCB. @Jason Rute
These are the same numbers as your chart above with “verified” instead of “no-GMP”. Are those the same thing?

Giving sokonanoda and nanoclo a try on the full proof. Fixed some performance issues in lean4export that allowed this. (Primary issue is that nat literals are output using an O(number_of_bits^2) algorithm. Fixing this reduces the export from estimated 15 hours down to <10 mins). Once I'm done having fun with all this I'll do a pass trying to make PRs some of these things to their appropriate projects (so far: this performance fix, and maybe adding some 4 color related stuff to mathlib, and a new benchmark in kernel arena)

My vague dream is that AI together with other systems (ML etc) could be used to explore the space of sets of configurations to try to find a nearly pareto optimal point that balances the overal complexity of the calculation per configuration, and the sheer number of them.

The point of this is that I'd like one day to organise a big in-person event that gathers hundreds of keen volunteers and have them do a purely-human check, replacing the computational part of the proof, as a kind of performance art/publicity stunt.
4CT, the Septuagint version

David Michael Roberts said:

The point of this is that I'd like one day to organise a big in-person event that gathers hundreds of keen volunteers and have them do a purely-human check, replacing the computational part of the proof, as a kind of performance art/publicity stunt.

I think @Kyle Miller once told me that if you would do this at the ICM, and cluster mathematicians to collaborate on the crowd-sourced computation, then you could not realistically expect them to be done by the end of the ICM, even if they spent all their time on it.

I might be misremembering. But I think this shows that the computation is really huge.

The proof would need further optimization, before you could do something like this.

I think that for the bigger graphs in the Robertson-Sanders-Seymour-Thomas list, checking reducibility is not something which can be done by a human, isn't it a huge calculation? I think the certificates are huge, you have to consider thousands of colourings and then do hundreds of Kempe chain arguments for each of them. And there are hundreds of graphs in the list.

well, the process is incredibly modular, no? Maybe it's a pipe-dream... I would do things like internationally organise schools, undergrad clubs etc. It wouldn't be a sit-down event or constrained to a single week in one place.
And I'd take a more modern proof than RSST

Some like Matt Parker (Stand-up Maths) would likely be interested in organizing something like this, if it were at all feasible. In 2024, he organized a hand calculation of 139 digits of pi, involving hundreds of people over several days. But before approaching Parker, someone should seriously scope out the project to estimate how many person-hours it would take. There also needs to be a plan for error-checking so that people can't just cheat and claim that something works out without actually checking.

Matt would be great for this kind of project and to be honest the only reason I didn't email him already about it was the fact that my understanding is that it is not currently feasible. But I might be out of date; I'm certainly not an expert in the field! It's just the kind of thing he would be able to get 100 people to sign up to for a weekend and my understanding is that this is nowhere near enough. IIRC the pi thing didn't go so well but we've discussed doing it again (he learnt some lessons from the first run), although "do something again" is never particularly exciting as a proposal, which is why 4CT is better if it could actually somehow be made to work.

There are two main parts to the proof, which we may call "reducibility" and "unavoidability." Most people are under the impression that the primary doubts about Appel and Haken's proof centered around the use of a computer, which was used to prove reducibility. But actually, the part of the proof that was most suspect was the unavoidability, which had to be done by hand, and was therefore error-prone. The 1989 book reports that someone tried to verify unavoidability, and got pretty far (uncovering one significant mistake in the process), but did not finish. Finishing that job might appeal to Matt Parker.

The RSST proof does not change the narrative all that much (nor does Gonthier's proof). Reducibility is still infeasible for a Matt-Parker-style effort. An important contribution by RSST was making the unavoidability part checkable by computer, but they also estimate that it could be done by hand with a few person-months, which is within reach of a Matt-Parker-style effort.

By the way, Parker's first couple of attempts to compute a significant number of digits of pi by hand were underwhelming, but his 2024 effort was a success, as I mentioned above.

Yes, his events inspired my dream.
The recent proof https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24880 linked above may be sufficiently different in its raw set of configurations and their type that they are "easier".
But more cases iirc.

Hi again. I’ve been continuing playing in this area. I got Claude to write a lean kernel that works more like coq. Which I’ve called lazylean: https://github.com/corun1024/lazylean . It passes all the correctness tests I could find, and I believe benchmarks favourably on kernel arena compared to lean, eink0rn and nanoclo(which has a somewhat similar technique I believe). I’m sorting out a PR to add it to kernel arena. I’ll need to do some more testing tho, so consider these results preliminary for now :-).

I then did a more direct port of the original coq proof, which lazylean is able to process in a reasonable-ish amount of time and memory. https://github.com/corun1024/4ct_direct_lean

This is a bit of a side project for me (since when was writing entire proof engines and 100k line proofs a “side project”?) and work is busy at the moment, I’ll try to make sure these are properly up to scratch when I get a bit of time so they might benefit others.

As a general comment on AI coding. It’s really getting to the point here that I feel the main value I can add is just thinking of interesting things to ask the AI to do. And then cleaning up the result a bit to make things more human.

This paper is a significant theoretical advance, but I don't think it helps as far as a Matt-Parker-style project is concerned. If I understand correctly, their computer check took a couple of hours on 256 cores.

I know they have a much larger set of configurations, but the block is how complex each one is to analyse, not how many there are. I'm very patient, and would do ten years of slow-burn with schools contributing one finished configuration, if need be. Not a one-shot event. :upside_down:
And generating the data would absolutely be done by machine, it's the running the check on every individual case I'd outsource to people, in an inversion of the usual approach here!

I'm very patient, and would do ten years of slow-burn with schools contributing one finished configuration, if need be.

So that's something on the order of 1 million person-hours, maybe? I haven't fully digested the newest paper, but it still looks to me that even with some kind of time-space tradeoff (getting the computers to produce certificates of some of the long computations), you're going to be many orders of magnitude off. Maybe you could write to Gonthier to see if he thinks that his version would be hand-checkable in 1 million person-hours.

In any case, I still think that such an effort should start with unavoidability, which should be feasible. Matt Parker would probably enjoy being able to announce that they were the first group in history to completely hand-check the hand-checkable part of the original Appel-Haken proof. It would be particularly fun if they were to find another serious bug; I'd personally guess that the chances are about 50%.

My next step, after recently talking with Andrew Stacey, would have been to talk to actual experts on the topic to see what the required effort would be. So I'm not going into this totally naively, but just hopefully.
